turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, it's... it's a lot of things, really, but I suppose the main reason I'm here, or at least the reason my wife and my director at work insisted I come in, is because I just can't seem to stop. I mean, I'm launching projects left and right, and it's not just little things. At work, I'm drawing up these massive, sweeping strategic plans for the entire IT department, and I'm simultaneously scheduling myself for three different advanced certifications that I don't even really need for my current role, but I just feel this incredible drive to do them, you know? And then I get home, and instead of relaxing, I'm completely overhauling our home network, running new ethernet cable through the walls, setting up redundant servers, which, frankly, is overkill for a three-bedroom house, but I just have to do it. And on top of all that, I'm messaging old contacts from college, from jobs I had ten years ago, pitching them ideas for startups or consulting gigs. It just gets so intense, this feeling of needing to accomplish everything right this second, that I just blow past all normal limits. I don't sleep, I barely eat, I just work and plan and build until my wife finally has to physically pull me away from the computer, or my director has to pull me into his office and tell me to stand down because I'm overwhelming the rest of the team. It's just... it's like a motor that won't shut off, no matter what I do.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had periods in your life where you felt the opposite—persistently down, drained of energy, or depressed?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah... yeah, it’s actually really jarring because, well, it’s like someone just unplugs the main server, you know? Complete system failure. I’ll go from running a hundred miles an hour, doing all those things I just mentioned, to just... stopping. It's a total crash. There are these long stretches where I wake up in the morning, and before I even open my eyes, I just feel like this completely failed version of myself. 

It’s hard to explain to people who haven't felt it, but it’s not just being sad, it’s this physical thing. I feel so incredibly heavy, like I'm made of lead, and just entirely flat inside. The contrast is what really gets me, because one week I'm taking on the world and redesigning the entire IT infrastructure, and the next, I'm lying there staring at the ceiling drywall, dreading the daylight. And it gets so bad that even just basic, everyday interactions become completely exhausting. Like, my wife will come into the bedroom and ask me something totally normal—just everyday stuff, like what I want for breakfast or if I remembered to pay the water bill—and just the idea of processing her words and answering her feels like entirely too much. It’s like climbing a mountain just to say 'I don't know.' I just lie there feeling useless and drained, which is so different from how I am when I'm wired, and I just can't seem to shake that heavy feeling no matter how much I sleep or how much my wife tries to encourage me to get out of bed... it's just this massive, crushing weight.

symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient notes that just processing words and answering simple questions feels like 'entirely too much', indicating diminished cognitive ability and mental exhaustion.

  "intent": "Determine whether the high periods have ever caused severe disruption to work or daily life, or required hospitalization, to distinguish hypomania from mania.",
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, it... it definitely causes problems. Big problems, honestly. I mean, at work, I actually got put on administrative leave recently, which is part of why my director wanted me here. It was this huge server migration project that I took over—well, I kind of forced my way into taking it over because I was convinced the original timeline was way too slow and conservative. I thought I could do it all in a single weekend, just me and a bunch of automated scripts I wrote at 3 AM. But, uh, I was moving so fast that I missed some critical dependencies, and the whole migration just... it failed completely. It was a disaster. Brought down the internal network for a day and a half, and my director had to pull me in and basically say I was a liability in that state, so they put me on mandatory leave. 

And it's not just work, it bleeds into everything. At home, my wife... bless her, she really tries, but she’s had to step in and basically act like a warden for my own good. She has to monitor our bank accounts because I'll just go online and spend thousands of dollars on new networking gear or software licenses without even thinking about our budget. She literally has to intervene with my late-night work binges, sometimes threatening to flip the main breaker just to get me off the computer. And, as you can imagine, that leads to these massive blowouts. We get into these intense arguments because I feel like she's stifling me, and my brain is just moving so fast that our conversations turn into me just talking over her, rapid-fire, until it turns into a huge fight. 

And then there's everything else I used to care about. I used to be really involved in things outside of the house. I played music at our church, you know, on the worship team, and I used to go indoor rock climbing a couple of times a week. I was even mentoring a few junior developers in the city... but I’ve completely pulled away from all of that. I just had to stop because I can't reliably show up for anyone anymore. When I'm revved up, I'm entirely consumed by my grand plans and I blow off band practice, and then when I crash, I can't even get out of bed to meet my climbing partner. I just leave people hanging over and over, so I eventually just stopped committing to anything at all because I never know if I'm going to be able to actually follow through. It just... it takes over everything.

turns.doctor_question: During these revved-up periods, have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, actually. It's... it's strange, and honestly, it's something I haven't really talked about much because it sounds so bizarre when you say it out loud, but yes. It happens mostly when I'm really wired, when I'm deep into one of those massive projects and I've been up for a day or two. You know how server rooms have that constant, low-level drone? That hum from all the fans and the cooling systems? Or even just in my home office, when I've got my own rig running hot and the house is completely quiet in the middle of the night. 

I'll be sitting there, just typing away, totally focused, and I'll hear... I'll hear things in the noise. At first, it's just my name. I'll hear someone say my name, clear as day, like they're standing right behind my chair. I'll spin around, fully expecting my wife to be standing there, maybe coming to check on me or tell me to come to bed, but the room is completely empty. And then it gets more specific. I'll hear these short, sharp comments mixed into the hum of the machines. Things like, 'check the logs,' just out of nowhere, or... or sometimes something more unsettling, like 'they know.' 

And I'll stop what I'm doing, and I'll take off my headphones, and I'll just listen, trying to figure out if it's coming from outside, or if maybe I left a video playing in a background tab, but there's nothing. It's just the fans spinning. But the voices, they sound so real, so distinct from the background noise, that I'll sometimes spend twenty minutes checking every corner of the house, looking out the windows, checking the security cameras, just trying to find the source. But there's never anyone there. It's just me, and the servers, and these voices that nobody else can hear. It's incredibly distracting, to be honest, because I'm trying to focus on these complex configurations, and I keep getting interrupted by these comments that seem to be coming right out of the hardware itself.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly describes hearing voices saying their name or phrases like 'check the logs' and 'they know' when no one else is present.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient mentions having been 'up for a day or two' during these revved-up periods, indicating a decreased need for sleep.
symptom_reasoning.S040: The patient describes being 'deep into one of those massive projects' and 'typing away, totally focused,' indicating an increase in goal-directed activity.
